question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

OSTENSIBLE
option_1: Genuine
option_2: Apparent
option_3: Concealed
option_4: Certain
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Apparent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ostensible (adjective) means stated or appearing to be true, but not necessarily so; outwardly professed. (घोषित, दिखावटी)
◦ Example: The ostensible purpose of the visit was trade, but the real aim was military.

 

• Apparent carries the same double edge — seeming real or true, though possibly not so. (प्रतीत होने वाला)
◦ Example: His apparent calm hid a deep anxiety.

 

• Both words describe the surface of a thing rather than its reality; that shared sense of 'seeming' makes them the closest pair here.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Genuine (वास्तविक, असली): truly what it is said to be — the opposite of ostensible.

 

• Option 3: Concealed (छिपा हुआ): kept hidden from view; ostensible things are on display, not hidden.

 

• Option 4: Certain (निश्चित): free from doubt — unrelated to appearance versus reality.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of ostensible frequently asked in SSC: seeming, professed, alleged, purported, superficial.

 

• Antonyms: actual, real, genuine, veritable.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

PERFUNCTORY
option_1: Thorough
option_2: Meticulous
option_3: Cursory
option_4: Painstaking
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cursory.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Perfunctory (adjective) means done merely as a duty, without interest, care or enthusiasm. (लापरवाही से किया गया, केवल औपचारिक)
◦ Example: The inspector gave the kitchen a perfunctory glance and signed the register.

 

• Cursory means hasty and superficial, without attention to detail — exactly the quality of a perfunctory act. (सरसरी, ऊपरी)
◦ Example: A cursory reading of the file will not reveal the discrepancy.

 

• The remaining three options all describe careful, complete work, which is the reverse of the required sense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Thorough (पूर्ण, संपूर्ण): complete with regard to every detail — an antonym.

 

• Option 2: Meticulous (अत्यंत सावधान): showing great attention to detail — an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Painstaking (मेहनती, श्रमसाध्य): done with great care and effort — an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of perfunctory: desultory, mechanical, offhand, token, casual.

 

• Here the three 'careful work' options — thorough, meticulous and painstaking — can be eliminated together as a single group, leaving only one candidate.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

ALACRITY
option_1: Eagerness
option_2: Promptness
option_3: Reluctance
option_4: Briskness
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Reluctance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alacrity (noun) means cheerful readiness and brisk willingness to act. (तत्परता, उत्साह)
◦ Example: She accepted the transfer with surprising alacrity.

 

• Its true opposite is reluctance — unwillingness or hesitation to do something. (अनिच्छा, हिचकिचाहट)
◦ Example: He agreed to testify only after months of reluctance.

 

• Note that alacrity combines two ideas — speed and willingness. Options 1, 2 and 4 each capture one of those ideas and are therefore synonyms, not antonyms.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Eagerness (उत्सुकता): keen desire to do something — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Promptness (शीघ्रता): acting without delay — a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Briskness (स्फूर्ति): quick and energetic manner — a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of alacrity: apathy, indifference, lethargy, disinclination, sluggishness.

 

• SSC often builds antonym questions with three synonyms and one antonym — spotting the majority pattern quickly narrows the field.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To carry coals to Newcastle
option_1: To undertake a hazardous journey for profit
option_2: To supply something to a place where it is already plentiful
option_3: To bring misfortune upon one's own household
option_4: To trade secretly with a rival
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To supply something to a place where it is already plentiful.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'To carry coals to Newcastle' means to do something completely pointless or superfluous — to take a commodity to a place that already has it in abundance. (व्यर्थ का प्रयास करना; जहाँ किसी वस्तु की पहले से बहुतायत हो, वहीं वही वस्तु ले जाना)
◦ Example: Sending textbooks to a publishing town is like carrying coals to Newcastle.

 

• The idiom is literal in origin: Newcastle upon Tyne in England was for centuries the greatest coal-exporting port in the country, so bringing coal to it was absurd.

 

• The Indian equivalent commonly cited is 'उलटे बांस बरेली को' — taking bamboo to Bareilly, a place already full of it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes a risky venture — idioms such as 'to sail close to the wind' convey that idea.

 

• Option 3 matches 'to bring a hornet's nest about one's ears', i.e. to invite trouble.

 

• Option 4 has no idiomatic connection with the given phrase; it is a plain distractor built from the word 'trade'.

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of futility often asked in SSC: to beat the air, to flog a dead horse, to plough the sands, to hold a candle to the sun.

question: Which is the correct spelling for 'the act of passing off another person's work or ideas as one's own'?
option_1: Plagiarism
option_2: Plagerism
option_3: Plagiarizm
option_4: Plaigarism
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Plagiarism.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Plagiarism (noun) is the practice of taking someone else's work, words or ideas and presenting them as one's own. (साहित्यिक चोरी)
◦ Example: The thesis was rejected on grounds of plagiarism.

 

• The correct sequence of letters is PLA - GIA - RISM. Two points decide the question:
◦ the vowel cluster is -gia-, not -ge- or -aiga-;
◦ the ending is -ism, spelt with s, never -izm.

 

• The word comes from Latin plagiarius, meaning 'kidnapper' — a plagiarist 'abducts' another's writing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Plagerism — wrong; the syllable -gia- has been reduced to -ge-.

 

• Option 3: Plagiarizm — wrong; the noun suffix -ism is never written with z in this word.

 

• Option 4: Plaigarism — wrong; the letters g and i have been transposed, giving plai-ga- in place of the correct pla-gia-.

 

NOTE

 

• Related forms: plagiarise/plagiarize (verb), plagiarist (noun, the person), plagiaristic (adjective).

question: Find the correctly spelled word meaning 'present, appearing or found everywhere'.
option_1: Ubiquitious
option_2: Ubiquitous
option_3: Ubiqitous
option_4: Ubiquituous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Ubiquitous.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ubiquitous (adjective) means existing or being everywhere at the same time; extremely common. (सर्वव्यापी)
◦ Example: Mobile phones have become ubiquitous even in remote villages.

 

• The correct division is U - BI - QUI - TOUS. The ending is the ordinary adjective suffix -ous, and the third syllable is qui, spelt q-u-i.

 

• It derives from Latin ubique, meaning 'everywhere'. The related noun is ubiquity.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Ubiquitious — wrong; an extra i has been inserted before -ous.

 

• Option 3: Ubiqitous — wrong; the u after q has been dropped, and in English q is almost always followed by u.

 

• Option 4: Ubiquituous — wrong; a superfluous u has been inserted, producing -tuous in place of the correct -tous.

 

NOTE

 

• Synonyms: omnipresent, pervasive, universal, widespread. Antonyms: rare, scarce, uncommon.

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A person who remains calm and unaffected by pleasure or pain'
option_1: Sceptic
option_2: Cynic
option_3: Stoic
option_4: Ascetic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Stoic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A stoic is a person who endures pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining, and who is equally unmoved by pleasure. (स्थितप्रज्ञ, समभावी, धैर्यवान)
◦ Example: He bore the loss of his savings with the calm of a true stoic.

 

• The word comes from Stoicism, the Greek school of philosophy founded by Zeno, which taught indifference to fortune and misfortune alike.

 

• The definition specifies indifference to both pleasure and pain, which rules out the three other options — each of them denotes a different mental attitude.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Sceptic (संशयवादी): one who habitually doubts accepted opinions or the possibility of certain knowledge.

 

• Option 2: Cynic (निंदक, दोषदर्शी): one who believes people are motivated purely by self-interest.

 

• Option 4: Ascetic (तपस्वी, संन्यासी): one who deliberately abstains from pleasure and practises severe self-discipline — close, but it stresses renunciation, not emotional steadiness.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish carefully: an ascetic gives up pleasure; a stoic may accept it but is not disturbed by its presence or absence.

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A statement that appears self-contradictory or absurd but may express a truth'
option_1: Oxymoron
option_2: Paradox
option_3: Anomaly
option_4: Euphemism
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Paradox.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself, yet on reflection may be found to be true. (विरोधाभास)
◦ Example: 'The child is father of the man' is a famous paradox from Wordsworth.

 

• The key element in the definition is self-contradiction at the level of a whole statement combined with an underlying truth.

 

• An oxymoron, by contrast, is a contradiction confined to two adjacent words — 'deafening silence', 'bitter-sweet'. Length and structure distinguish the two.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Oxymoron (विरोधाभासी युग्म): a figure of speech joining two contradictory terms.

 

• Option 3: Anomaly (विसंगति): something that deviates from what is standard or expected — an irregularity, not a statement.

 

• Option 4: Euphemism (मृदूक्ति): a mild or indirect expression used in place of a harsh one, e.g. 'passed away' for 'died'.

 

NOTE

 

• Frequently confused literary terms in SSC: paradox, oxymoron, irony, hyperbole, understatement (litotes).

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct correlative to complete the inversion structure.

 

Scarcely had the ceremony begun _____ the power supply failed.
option_1: than
option_2: when
option_3: then
option_4: that
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. when.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• English fixes the correlative of each 'almost immediately after' structure. The pairs must not be mixed:
◦ Scarcely ... when
◦ Hardly ... when
◦ No sooner ... than

 

• Since the sentence opens with Scarcely, the only permissible correlative is when. The full sentence reads: Scarcely had the ceremony begun when the power supply failed.

 

• Note the inversion that these negative adverbials force: the auxiliary had moves before the subject the ceremony. The first clause takes the past perfect and the second the simple past.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: than — belongs with no sooner, not with scarcely.

 

• Option 3: then — an adverb of time; it cannot introduce the subordinate clause here.

 

• Option 4: that — cannot serve as the correlative of scarcely; it belongs to the degree/result patterns 'so ... that' and 'such ... that'.

 

NOTE

 

• Other adverbials that trigger inversion: Never, Seldom, Rarely, Little, Not only, Under no circumstances, Not until.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Despite of the heavy rainfall (1)/ that lashed the coastal districts, (2)/ the relief teams managed to reach (3)/ the marooned villages before nightfall. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Despite is itself a preposition and is therefore never followed by of. The correct form is 'Despite the heavy rainfall'.

 

• The confusion arises from 'in spite of', which is a three-word prepositional phrase and does require of. The two structures must not be blended:
◦ Despite + noun/gerund — Despite the delay, we reached on time.
◦ In spite of + noun/gerund — In spite of the delay, we reached on time.

 

• The corrected sentence: Despite the heavy rainfall that lashed the coastal districts, the relief teams managed to reach the marooned villages before nightfall.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct — the relative pronoun that properly introduces the defining clause modifying 'rainfall'.

 

• Part (3) is correct — manage is regularly followed by the to-infinitive.

 

• Part (4) is correct — before nightfall is an idiomatic time expression requiring no article.

 

NOTE

 

• The same trap appears with 'discuss about', 'order for', 'demand for' (verb), 'reach at' — all of which take no preposition.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The number of applicants (1)/ who have qualified for the final interview (2)/ are considerably higher (3)/ than the department had anticipated. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the main clause is 'The number', which is singular. It therefore requires the singular verb is, not are. Part (3) should read 'is considerably higher'.

 

• Remember the contrast:
◦ The number of + plural noun + singular verb — The number of students is rising.
◦ A number of + plural noun + plural verb — A number of students are absent.

 

• The plural noun applicants in between is only part of the prepositional phrase and can never govern the main verb — this is the classic 'intervening phrase' trap.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct — here the relative pronoun who refers to applicants (plural), so the plural verb have qualified is right. Note how the two verbs in the sentence legitimately differ in number.

 

• Part (1) and Part (4) are grammatically sound; had anticipated correctly shows the earlier of two past situations.

 

NOTE

 

• Similar singular-subject expressions: the quantity of, the amount of, the total of, one of, each of, every one of.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

The committee has approved the revised budget.
option_1: The revised budget was approved by the committee.
option_2: The revised budget has been approved by the committee.
option_3: The revised budget is approved by the committee.
option_4: The revised budget had been approved by the committee.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The revised budget has been approved by the committee.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The active sentence is in the present perfect tense (has approved). The passive of the present perfect is formed as:
◦ has/have been + past participle (V3)

 

• Steps applied here:
◦ Object the revised budget becomes the subject.
◦ has approved → has been approved.
◦ Subject the committee becomes the agent with by.

 

• The resulting sentence keeps the original tense intact: The revised budget has been approved by the committee.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 shifts the tense to the simple past (was approved) — tense must never change in voice conversion.

 

• Option 3 gives the simple present passive (is approved).

 

• Option 4 gives the past perfect passive (had been approved), which corresponds to the active 'had approved'.

 

NOTE

 

• Quick reference: Simple Present → is/am/are + V3; Present Continuous → is/am/are being + V3; Present Perfect → has/have been + V3; Simple Past → was/were + V3; Simple Future → will be + V3; Future Perfect → will have been + V3.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The trophy was being polished by the caretaker when the guests arrived.
option_1: The caretaker polished the trophy when the guests arrived.
option_2: The caretaker was polishing the trophy when the guests arrived.
option_3: The caretaker had polished the trophy when the guests arrived.
option_4: The caretaker has been polishing the trophy when the guests arrived.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The caretaker was polishing the trophy when the guests arrived.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the past continuous passive — was being + polished (V3). Its active counterpart must be the past continuous active — was/were + V-ing.

 

• Steps applied here:
◦ The agent the caretaker becomes the subject.
◦ was being polished → was polishing.
◦ The trophy becomes the object.

 

• The subordinate clause when the guests arrived contains no passive verb and therefore stays unchanged — only the main clause is converted.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses the simple past and loses the sense of an action in progress at the moment of arrival.

 

• Option 3 uses the past perfect, which would wrongly mean the polishing was finished before the guests came.

 

• Option 4 uses the present perfect continuous, which cannot combine with the past-time clause 'when the guests arrived'.

 

NOTE

 

• Continuous tenses in the passive always insert being between the auxiliary and V3; there is no passive form for perfect continuous tenses in standard usage.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homonym of the highlighted word.

 

The batsman replaced his bat before the start of the second innings.
option_1: He tapped the bat on the crease before facing the delivery.
option_2: The willow bat had been oiled twice that season.
option_3: A bat flitted silently through the twilight above the orchard.
option_4: The captain chose a lighter bat for the shorter format.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. A bat flitted silently through the twilight above the orchard.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word spelt and pronounced identically to another but carrying an entirely different and unrelated meaning. (समनामी शब्द)

 

• In the given sentence, bat means the wooden implement used to strike the ball in cricket. The question therefore asks for the sentence in which the same spelling carries a different meaning.

 

• Option 3 uses bat to mean a small nocturnal flying mammal. The verb flitted and the setting twilight above the orchard confirm this second sense, so it is the required homonym.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1, Option 2 and Option 4 all use bat in the same cricketing sense as the highlighted word, so none of them is a homonym — they merely repeat the original meaning.

 

• Bat also works as a verb, both in cricket ('India batted first') and in the idiom 'without batting an eyelid', meaning without showing any surprise.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not confuse the terms: homonyms are alike in spelling and sound (bank, bat, bark); homophones sound alike but are spelt differently (canon/cannon, principal/principle); homographs are spelt alike but may differ in pronunciation (lead, tear, bow).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The research team has finally made a headway in decoding the inscription.
option_1: made headway
option_2: made the headway
option_3: made headways
option_4: make a headway
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. made headway.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Headway is an uncountable noun meaning forward movement or progress. (प्रगति, आगे बढ़ना)

 

• Being uncountable, it takes no article a/an and has no plural form. The fixed collocation is 'to make headway'.
◦ Example: The talks made little headway in the first round.

 

• The corrected sentence: The research team has finally made headway in decoding the inscription.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: made the headway — the definite article is equally unidiomatic in this fixed phrase.

 

• Option 3: made headways — an uncountable noun cannot be pluralised.

 

• Option 4: make a headway — doubly wrong: it retains the article and breaks the perfect tense begun by has.

 

NOTE

 

• Other uncountable nouns that are wrongly given articles or plurals in exams: information, advice, luggage, furniture, machinery, scenery, progress, equipment, evidence.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Few inventions have reshaped ordinary life as quietly as the mechanical clock. Before its spread across late-medieval Europe, time was read from the sky and from the seasons: the working day expanded in summer and contracted in winter, and the hour itself was an elastic unit. Monastic communities, obliged to pray at fixed intervals, were among the first to demand a device that could divide the day impartially, and it was from the cloister that the machine passed to the town. Once installed in a civic tower, the clock ceased to be an aid to devotion and became an instrument of coordination. Markets opened and closed by it; wages were reckoned against it; the bell that had once summoned the faithful now summoned the labourer.

 

The consequences were not merely practical but moral. A society that measures time in identical units begins to treat it as a quantity that can be saved, spent or squandered, and punctuality, once an eccentricity, hardened into a virtue. Employers who paid by the hour acquired a powerful interest in ensuring that the hour was honestly filled, and the disputes over the length of the working day that convulsed the nineteenth century were possible only because both sides could appeal to the same impartial dial. What appeared to be a neutral instrument thus quietly redistributed authority: whoever controlled the clock controlled the rhythm of other people's lives.

 

Nor did the older rhythms disappear without protest. Agricultural labour, tied to weather and daylight, resisted the tyranny of the timetable, and the standardisation of time across regions — driven, in the nineteenth century, by the demands of the railway rather than by any philosophical argument — was resented as an intrusion by a distant authority. Yet the resistance failed, less because the arguments against it were weak than because commerce and transport could no longer function without a common measure. The clock did not simply record time; it manufactured a shared and enforceable version of it, and in doing so made possible the coordinated, impersonal society we now take for granted.

 

According to the passage, why were monastic communities among the first to require a mechanical timekeeper?
option_1: They wished to regulate the opening and closing of markets.
option_2: They were obliged to offer prayers at fixed intervals of the day.
option_3: They wanted to free the working day from the influence of the seasons.
option_4: They were required to pay their labourers by the hour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. They were obliged to offer prayers at fixed intervals of the day.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states directly: 'Monastic communities, obliged to pray at fixed intervals, were among the first to demand a device that could divide the day impartially.'

 

• The motive identified is therefore religious discipline — a fixed prayer routine that the variable natural day could not serve.

 

• This is a factual/detail question; the answer is stated in the text and needs no inference beyond locating the relevant sentence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes what happened after the clock moved to the civic tower, not the monastic motive.

 

• Option 3 reverses the logic — freedom from seasonal variation was a consequence of the clock, not the monks' stated aim.

 

• Option 4 relates to employers in the second paragraph and has nothing to do with the cloister.

 

NOTE

 

• In detail-based questions, prefer the option that echoes the passage's own wording; options that describe later effects are typical distractors.

What change does the passage describe once the clock was installed in a civic tower?
option_1: It became more accurate than the monastic devices that preceded it.
option_2: It turned from an aid to worship into an instrument of economic coordination.
option_3: It lost public support because townspeople resented its bells.
option_4: It replaced the calendar as the chief measure of the agricultural year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It turned from an aid to worship into an instrument of economic coordination.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage says: 'Once installed in a civic tower, the clock ceased to be an aid to devotion and became an instrument of coordination.'

 

• The illustrations that follow — markets opening and closing by it, wages reckoned against it, the bell summoning the labourer instead of the faithful — establish that the new function was economic and civic.

 

• The shift described is therefore one of purpose, not of technology or accuracy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces accuracy, which the passage never discusses.

 

• Option 3 contradicts the text; resistance is mentioned only in connection with agricultural labour and regional standardisation, not with the town clock's bells.

 

• Option 4 brings in the calendar, which does not appear in the passage at all.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch for distractors that are plausible in the real world but absent from the passage; comprehension answers must rest on the text alone.

What appeared to be a neutral instrument thus quietly redistributed authority: whoever controlled the clock controlled the rhythm of other people's lives.

 

Nor did the older rhythms disappear without protest. Agricultural labour, tied to weather and daylight, resisted the tyranny of the timetable, and the standardisation of time across regions — driven, in the nineteenth century, by the demands of the railway rather than by any philosophical argument — was resented as an intrusion by a distant authority. Yet the resistance failed, less because the arguments against it were weak than because commerce and transport could no longer function without a common measure. The clock did not simply record time; it manufactured a shared and enforceable version of it, and in doing so made possible the coordinated, impersonal society we now take for granted.

 

What does the expression 'the hour itself was an elastic unit' most nearly imply?
option_1: The hour was measured differently by each monastery.
option_2: The length of an hour varied according to the season and daylight.
option_3: People were permitted to arrive late for appointments.
option_4: The hour was too short to be of any practical use.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The length of an hour varied according to the season and daylight.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The clue lies in the sentence immediately before: 'the working day expanded in summer and contracted in winter, and the hour itself was an elastic unit.'

 

• Elastic here is used figuratively to mean capable of stretching and shrinking. Applied to the hour, it means the unit had no fixed duration and followed the length of daylight.

 

• This is an inference/vocabulary-in-context question: the meaning of 'elastic' must be drawn from the surrounding contrast between summer and winter.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 limits the variation to monasteries, whereas the passage describes a general practice of reading time from the sky.

 

• Option 3 confuses the flexibility of the unit of measurement with flexibility in human punctuality.

 

• Option 4 misreads 'elastic' as 'short'; the passage makes no claim about the hour being useless.

 

NOTE

 

• For vocabulary-in-context items, always substitute the option back into the sentence and test whether the logic of the paragraph still holds.

Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

Once installed in a civic tower, the clock ceased to be an aid to devotion and became an instrument of coordination. Markets opened and closed by it; wages were reckoned against it; the bell that had once summoned the faithful now summoned the labourer.

 

The consequences were not merely practical but moral. A society that measures time in identical units begins to treat it as a quantity that can be saved, spent or squandered, and punctuality, once an eccentricity, hardened into a virtue. Employers who paid by the hour acquired a powerful interest in ensuring that the hour was honestly filled, and the disputes over the length of the working day that convulsed the nineteenth century were possible only because both sides could appeal to the same impartial dial. What appeared to be a neutral instrument thus quietly redistributed authority: whoever controlled the clock controlled the rhythm of other people's lives.

 

Nor did the older rhythms disappear without protest. Agricultural labour, tied to weather and daylight, resisted the tyranny of the timetable, and the standardisation of time across regions — driven, in the nineteenth century, by the demands of the railway rather than by any philosophical argument — was resented as an intrusion by a distant authority. Yet the resistance failed, less because the arguments against it were weak than because commerce and transport could no longer function without a common measure. The clock did not simply record time; it manufactured a shared and enforceable version of it, and in doing so made possible the coordinated, impersonal society we now take for granted.

 

According to the passage, what made the nineteenth-century disputes over the length of the working day possible?
option_1: Workers had begun to own clocks of their own.
option_2: Employers had voluntarily reduced the hours of labour.
option_3: Both sides could appeal to the same impartial measure of time.
option_4: The railway had made travel to the workplace faster.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Both sides could appeal to the same impartial measure of time.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states: 'the disputes over the length of the working day that convulsed the nineteenth century were possible only because both sides could appeal to the same impartial dial.'

 

• The argument is that a shared, neutral standard is a precondition of disagreement — without a common measure, employer and worker would have had no common ground on which to quarrel.

 

• The word 'only' in the original sentence marks this as the necessary condition, which is exactly what the question asks for.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is not mentioned; the passage speaks of the civic tower clock, a public instrument, not private ownership.

 

• Option 2 contradicts the passage, which says employers had a powerful interest in seeing the hour honestly filled.

 

• Option 4 misplaces the railway, which the passage links to the standardisation of time across regions, not to working-hour disputes.

 

NOTE

 

• Questions built on the phrase 'possible only because' test cause and condition; locate the causal connective in the text before choosing.

Yet the resistance failed, less because the arguments against it were weak than because commerce and transport could no longer function without a common measure. The clock did not simply record time; it manufactured a shared and enforceable version of it, and in doing so made possible the coordinated, impersonal society we now take for granted.

 

What does the author suggest about the standardisation of time across regions?
option_1: It was accepted readily because its philosophical justification was persuasive.
option_2: It succeeded because commerce and transport could no longer function without a common measure.
option_3: It was imposed by monasteries seeking uniform hours of prayer.
option_4: It failed wherever agricultural labour remained dominant.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It succeeded because commerce and transport could no longer function without a common measure.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage says the resistance failed 'less because the arguments against it were weak than because commerce and transport could no longer function without a common measure.'

 

• The construction 'less because X than because Y' places the real cause in Y — practical necessity — while conceding that the opposing arguments were not, in themselves, feeble.

 

• The passage also notes that standardisation was driven 'by the demands of the railway rather than by any philosophical argument', reinforcing the same point.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is the exact reverse of the text, which expressly denies a philosophical motive.

 

• Option 3 transfers the monastic role from the first paragraph to a nineteenth-century development.

 

• Option 4 overstates the case: agricultural labour resisted, but the passage says the resistance failed.

 

NOTE

 

• Comparative constructions such as 'less because ... than because ...', 'not so much ... as' and 'rather than' are favourite devices in SSC comprehension; read them slowly to identify which clause carries the emphasis.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The manager said to me, “Have you submitted the audit report?”
option_1: The manager asked me have I submitted the audit report.
option_2: The manager asked me whether I had submitted the audit report.
option_3: The manager asked me that had I submitted the audit report.
option_4: The manager said me if I have submitted the audit report.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The manager asked me whether I had submitted the audit report.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The quoted sentence is a yes/no interrogative. Three rules apply together:
◦ The reporting verb said to changes to asked.
◦ Since there is no question word, the connective must be if or whether.
◦ The interrogative order is dropped: the clause becomes a statement — subject before verb.

 

• Backshift of tense is also required: have you submitted (present perfect) → had submitted (past perfect).

 

• The pronoun you refers to the listener 'me' and therefore becomes I. No question mark is retained.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 retains the interrogative word order ('have I submitted') and omits the connective.

 

• Option 3 wrongly uses that for a question and keeps the inverted order.

 

• Option 4 uses said me (ungrammatical — it must be 'said to me' or 'told me') and fails to backshift 'have' to 'had'.

 

NOTE

 

• For wh-questions the question word itself serves as the connective — *He asked what I was doing* — and if/whether must not be added.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

The teacher said, “Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.”
option_1: The teacher said that water boiled at one hundred degrees Celsius.
option_2: The teacher said that water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.
option_3: The teacher told that water had boiled at one hundred degrees Celsius.
option_4: The teacher said water would boil at one hundred degrees Celsius.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The teacher said that water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported clause states a universal truth / scientific fact. Such statements are exempt from backshift — the present tense is retained even though the reporting verb is in the past.
◦ Example: He said that the earth revolves round the sun.

 

• The reporting verb said is correctly followed by the conjunction that with no object, and the inverted commas are removed.

 

• Hence boils stays as boils, and the sentence becomes: The teacher said that water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is not ungrammatical in itself, but by the convention followed in competitive examinations a universal or scientific truth retains the present tense even after a past reporting verb; Option 2 is therefore the required answer.

 

• Option 3 is doubly wrong: told requires an object ('told us'), and the past perfect is inappropriate for a permanent truth.

 

• Option 4 turns a fact into a prediction with would boil.

 

NOTE

 

• Other cases where the tense does not change: habitual facts, historical facts with a stated time, and sentences containing 'if' clauses of the second and third type.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

The priest prayed that the village might be spared the epidemic.
option_1: “The village may be spared the epidemic,” said the priest.
option_2: “May the village be spared the epidemic!” prayed the priest.
option_3: “Let the village spare the epidemic,” the priest prayed.
option_4: “The village might be spared the epidemic,” the priest prayed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. “May the village be spared the epidemic!” prayed the priest.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb prayed together with the structure 'that ... might' marks this as an optative sentence — one that expresses a wish, prayer or blessing.

 

• In converting an optative from indirect to direct speech:
◦ The clause opens with May placed before the subject.
◦ The sentence closes with an exclamation mark.
◦ Might reverts to may, since the direct words were spoken in the present.

 

• The reporting verb prayed (or 'wished') is retained outside the quotation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the ordinary statement order and loses the optative form and the exclamation mark.

 

• Option 3 reverses the meaning entirely — it makes the village the agent that spares the epidemic.

 

• Option 4 retains might, which belongs to the indirect version, and again omits the optative inversion.

 

NOTE

 

• Typical optative patterns: May you live long! May God bless you! Long live the Republic! In indirect speech they take wished/prayed that ... might.

question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a meaningful passage.

 

1. Such survivors multiply and pass on their resistant traits to later generations.
2. Antibiotic resistance arises when bacteria withstand the very drugs designed to destroy them.
3. Hence physicians now advocate strict limits on the prescription of these medicines.
4. Over time even ordinary infections become difficult to treat.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 2-1-4-3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 2 is the opening sentence: it introduces the topic — antibiotic resistance — and defines it. A definition of the key term almost always comes first.

 

• Sentence 1 must follow, because the phrase 'Such survivors' is a backward reference to the bacteria that 'withstand the drugs' in sentence 2. It cannot stand without that antecedent.

 

• Sentence 4 states the result of the multiplication described in sentence 1, marked by the time expression 'Over time'.

 

• Sentence 3 is the conclusion, signalled by the connective 'Hence', which introduces the recommended remedy.

 

• The logical chain is therefore definition → mechanism → consequence → prescription: 2-1-4-3.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (2-4-1-3) breaks the link between 'Such survivors' and its antecedent by inserting sentence 4 in between.

 

• Option 3 (1-2-4-3) opens with a demonstrative reference that has nothing to refer back to.

 

• Option 4 (4-2-1-3) begins with a consequence before the phenomenon has been introduced.

 

NOTE

 

• Useful signposts in rearrangement questions: demonstratives (such, this, these, it) point backwards; connectives (hence, therefore, thus) mark conclusions; definitions and general statements usually open the passage.

question:
Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a logical passage.

 

1. Their loss therefore leaves shorelines far more exposed than is generally realised.
2. Mangroves, for instance, trap sediment and blunt the force of storm surges.
3. Coastal wetlands are often dismissed as unproductive wasteland.
4. Yet they perform protective functions that engineered defences replicate only at great cost.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. 3-4-2-1.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 3 opens the passage: it presents the general belief about coastal wetlands and introduces the subject of the paragraph.

 

• Sentence 4 follows immediately, because 'Yet' signals a contrast with that dismissive view, and 'they' refers back to the wetlands of sentence 3.

 

• Sentence 2 supplies the example that supports sentence 4 — the phrase 'for instance' shows it must come after the general claim it illustrates.

 

• Sentence 1 concludes with the inference, marked by 'therefore' and by 'Their loss', which presupposes that the value of wetlands has already been established.

 

• The structure is claim → contrast → illustration → conclusion: 3-4-2-1.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (3-2-4-1) places the example before the general statement it is meant to illustrate.

 

• Option 2 (4-3-2-1) begins with a contrastive 'Yet', which cannot open a paragraph.

 

• Option 4 (2-3-4-1) starts with a specific instance while the topic itself is still unintroduced.

 

NOTE

 

• A sentence beginning with Yet, But, However, Therefore, Hence, Moreover or For instance can almost never be the first sentence of a rearranged passage.
